title: Trace readers across a write-ahead log commit
summary: Separate committed state, reader snapshots and checkpoint progress.
objectives: Trace old and new reader snapshots across a commit.
Explain the role of a checkpoint.
Identify why an active WAL is part of database state.

blocks.title: Prerequisites and subject boundary
blocks.text: Prerequisites: transactions, files and process resources. Storage-engine behavior belongs here; C++ buffers and locks are implementation mechanisms.

In SQLite WAL mode, changes are appended to a write-ahead log, and a commit record establishes a completed transaction. A reader remembers an end mark and consults committed page versions no later than that mark. A checkpoint moves eligible log content back into the database file; it is not the same event as committing a transaction. Long-lived readers can constrain checkpoint progress. The WAL therefore participates in persistent database state and must not be casually detached from a live database file. Durability under power failure also depends on documented synchronization settings and storage behavior, not simply the existence of a log.

Our original finite model tracks one logical record called stock. Its committed value starts at eight. Reader R1 begins before a writer changes stock to five. Reader R2 begins after that writer successfully commits. Assume WAL mode, valid storage, and no other transactions. We describe visible values rather than low-level page numbers.

blocks.caption: Original worked trace; finite assumptions, not executable platform code
blocks.code:
R1 begins: snapshot end mark E0, stock=8
Writer appends stock=5 and commits at E1
R1 reads again: stock=8 from its existing snapshot
R2 begins at E1: stock=5
R1 ends: its old-snapshot requirement is released
Checkpoint can make further progress subject to other readers.

blocks.text: Both readers can be correct at the same wall-clock moment because they observe different committed snapshots. R1 is not required to change mid-transaction when R2 sees five. The checkpoint consolidates storage while preserving the visibility obligations of active readers. Treating the database file alone as the entire current state could miss committed changes still residing in the WAL. Use the database’s supported backup or checkpoint workflow instead of assembling an assumed snapshot by copying files independently.

Have R1 remain open while many later writes commit and explain why this can retain old storage obligations. Then end R1 and start a fresh read transaction; under the stated schedule it observes the newer committed value. Measure reader lifetime and checkpoint behavior before changing tuning parameters. A larger log is an operational symptom to investigate, not an invitation to delete it manually.

blocks.prompt: Does a commit have to wait until its changed pages are copied into the main database file before a new reader can see them?
blocks.explanation: No. In WAL mode a new reader can use the committed log content appropriate to its end mark. Checkpointing transfers eligible content later. The distinction is central to concurrent readers and writers, while the exact durability guarantees still depend on the configured synchronization and underlying storage.
